title: the one at every doorway
hook: an elephant-headed figure on the dashboard, by the door, at the top of the page

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranam: the bow, and the blessing that comes back. Your line was bow to what came before you. Did you thank someone? Today you meet someone. Day six.

A small statue glued to a taxi dashboard, nodding over every pothole. A picture above a shop counter. A carved figure beside a front door. On a wedding invitation, sometimes just his name, printed at the very top before anyone else's. Elephant head. Round belly. One tusk whole, one broken. He sits where things start: doorways, first pages, first days. His name is Ganesha. To someone meeting him for the first time, an elephant-headed god can look strange. Give it a few minutes, and he turns out to stand for something easy to want at the start of anything hard. Someone to clear the road.
screen: `THE DASHBOARD. THE DOOR. THE FIRST PAGE.` → `ELEPHANT HEAD, ONE TUSK.` → `WHERE THINGS START.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. He has another name too, Ganapati, which means much the same thing. But the title that explains the doorway is this one: Vighnaharta. Vighna is an obstacle. Harta is one who removes. The remover of obstacles. That's why he's honored first. Before a ceremony, before a wedding, before a new shop opens its shutters or a student sits down to an exam, Ganesha is invoked at the start. Some people write a short line at the top of a page before they begin: shri ganeshaya namah. Listen to that last word. Namah. It's the same bow you learned on day one, in namaste. A bow to Ganesha, before the work. How he got the elephant's head is a story, and a good one, and you'll hear it later on this path. Today, just look at him. There's a popular way of reading his body. Big ears: listen more than you talk. Small eyes: focus. Big belly: take in whatever life serves you, the good and the hard. And the broken tusk. Tradition says Ganesha wrote down the Mahabharata as the sage Vyasa spoke it, and one story people tell says that when his pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing. In the Puranas he is also a guardian of thresholds, and the same lord who removes obstacles can place them too. At a doorway, people ask him for the first: a clear way in.
screen: `GANESHA — LORD OF THE GANAS.` · `VIGHNAHARTA — REMOVER OF OBSTACLES.` · `HONORED FIRST, BEFORE THE WORK.` · `BIG EARS, SMALL EYES, ONE TUSK.` · then, large: `CLEAR THE ROAD, THEN BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Find something near you that marks a start: a door, a laptop lid, the cover of a notebook. Rest a hand on it. Let one thing you're about to begin this week come to mind. With the bell, name what's in the way, quietly, just once: fear, time, a person, an excuse. Then ask for the road to be clear, in whatever way fits you. Some who pray begin with his name: shri ganeshaya namah. Or just picture the road, open. Breathe out, and lift your hand.
Ganesha. Lord of the ganas, remover of obstacles, the one at the door. Sixth word, and the first name on your strand.
Your line: clear the road, then begin. Today, before the next thing you start, take one second and name what's in the way. Then begin. That's day six.

screen: `DAY 6 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A HANDRAIL MADE OF SOUND.`

howItsDone: Hindus honor Ganesha first at ceremonies, weddings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

original.note: Sanskrit: gana, the attendants, plus isha, lord. lord of the ganas.

trapdoor: what you thought: an elephant god for good luck.
what it means: the remover of obstacles, honored first, at the door of beginnings.
what a scholar hears: gana + isha, lord of Shiva's attendants; also Vighnaharta. tradition makes him the scribe of the Mahabharata as Vyasa dictated.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 1 (Ganesha as scribe for Vyasa)

notes: The Ganesha-as-scribe episode appears in some recensions of the Mahabharata's Adi Parva and is not in the Critical Edition's main text; the script says 'tradition says'. The tusk-as-pen story is given as 'one story people tell'. Confirm.
Body symbolism (ears, eyes, belly) is given as 'a popular way of reading the body', not scripture. Confirm.
The birth and elephant-head story is deliberately held back: it is told in full on days 22–24 (Shiva Purana).
Vighnaharta transliterated as commonly written; Sanskrit vighnahartṛ. Confirm.

Cut from manuscript day 6 under the claims rule: 'walk into almost any Indian home', 'the most recognizable figure in the tradition', 'every wedding, every new business, every exam', 'the one most kids hear', 'a billion people', and 'five thousand years of people'.
Title keeps the index's 'every doorway'; the script itself says doorways, not every one.

Audit pass: cut 'not a guard who keeps you out', which a scholar would catch: Ganesha is a threshold guardian (he guards Parvati's door in the Shiva Purana story told on days 22–24) and is also Vighnakarta, who places obstacles. The teach now says both, briefly, without telling the birth story early. Confirm wording.

Editor pass: practice rewritten around a hand on something that marks a start (a door, a laptop lid, a notebook), so it no longer repeats the three-breath first/second/third template of days 3–5; same content (name the obstacle, ask for a clear road, optional shri ganeshaya namah). Checked the gana + isha, Ganapati and Vighnaharta glosses; no other changes.
